one_liner: A narrow-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.2x fair value. Interesting below about $683.

profile.what: United Rentals rents construction and industrial equipment from branches across North America, including general machinery and speciality lines such as power, trench safety and fluid solutions.
profile.money: It buys equipment, rents it many times over and sells it used. Profit depends on how much of the fleet is on rent and at what rate.
profile.valued: United Rentals is valued on EV/EBITDA and free cash flow. The multiple moves with construction activity and confidence in large projects.

summary.sentence: The largest equipment renter: scale advantages on a debt-financed fleet.
strengths: Revenue has grown every year in the record.
Operating cash flow has grown strongly over the record.
risks: Debt is well above shareholders' equity.
Gross margin has slipped for three years.
Most operating cash flow goes back into the fleet.

meaning.what_it_does: The largest equipment-rental company in North America, renting machinery such as lifts, excavators and power equipment to construction and industrial customers.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Rental fees on a very large fleet, plus sales of used equipment.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Its scale lets it buy equipment cheaply and keep it rented across many sites; more customers now rent instead of owning.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Construction falls sharply while it carries a large, debt-financed fleet.

moat.summary: Much larger than any rival, which helps purchasing and fleet use, but rental rates are set by a competitive market.

industry.summary: Equipment rental changes slowly; demand follows construction and large industrial projects.

management.summary: Has grown through well-executed acquisitions and returns surplus cash through buybacks and a newer dividend.

financial_health.ratio_gaps: Not available from the data source, so not shown: a ten-year record, inventory and receivables turnover, the quick ratio, goodwill and tangible book value, and maintenance capex split from growth capex. Owner earnings therefore deduct all capex, which is conservative.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow, capex held at depreciation: $4.4B a year: operating cash flow less depreciation and stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). Capex is running at 8.7x depreciation, so most of it is expansion, not upkeep. (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 5–11% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 26%; cost of capital 8.8%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
